description: Congee with Century Egg is a quintessential Chinese comfort food, a warm and creamy rice porridge often enjoyed for breakfast or as a light meal. This traditional dish features tender rice cooked until velvety smooth, beautifully complemented by the unique, savory flavor of preserved century eggs. Garnished with fresh ginger and green onions, it offers a harmonious blend of textures and tastes that is both nourishing and deeply satisfying.

instructions.title: Prepare the Rice
instructions.text: Wash the rice thoroughly under cold running water until the water runs clear. For an extra creamy congee, you can marinate the washed rice with 1 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of cooking oil for at least 30 minutes, or even freeze it overnight.

instructions.title: Prepare Century Eggs and Ginger
instructions.text: Carefully peel the century eggs and dice them into small, bite-sized pieces. Peel the fresh ginger and cut it into thin julienne strips. Set aside a small portion of both for garnish later.

instructions.title: Start Cooking the Congee
instructions.text: In a large pot, bring 8-10 cups of water or chicken broth to a rolling boil over high heat. Add the prepared rice to the boiling liquid. Stir well to prevent sticking. Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover, and let it simmer.

instructions.title: Simmer Until Creamy
instructions.text: Continue to simmer the congee for at least 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom of the pot. The longer it simmers, the creamier and thicker the congee will become. Add more hot water if the congee becomes too thick.

instructions.title: Add Century Eggs and Seasoning
instructions.text: Once the congee has reached your desired creamy consistency, stir in most of the diced century eggs and julienned ginger. Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Cook for another 5 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld.

instructions.title: Serve and Garnish
instructions.text: Ladle the hot congee into individual serving bowls. Garnish with the reserved diced century eggs, julienned ginger, and chopped green onions. Drizzle with a few drops of sesame oil if desired. Serve immediately and enjoy this comforting Chinese breakfast.

tips: For extra creamy congee, freeze the washed rice overnight before cooking. This helps break down the starch faster and achieve a smoother texture.
To reduce the strong ammonia smell sometimes associated with century eggs, soak them in water for about 30 minutes before peeling and dicing.
Congee thickens as it cools; if reheating, add a little hot water or broth to achieve the desired consistency and stir well.
article:
Congee with Century Egg: The Ultimate Chinese Comfort Breakfast

Imagine a bowl of silken, warm rice porridge, subtly seasoned, with tender pieces of lean pork and the distinct, savory depth of century eggs. This isn't just breakfast; it's a hug in a bowl, a staple of Chinese cuisine that transcends mere sustenance to become a comforting ritual. Congee with Century Egg, known in Cantonese as "pidan shourou zhou" (皮蛋瘦肉粥), is a quintessential Chinese breakfast recipe cherished for its nourishing qualities, unique flavors, and incredible ease of digestion. Whether you're seeking a hearty start to your day, a soothing meal when you're under the weather, or simply an authentic taste of Chinese tradition, this dish delivers. Let's delve into the world of this beloved porridge and learn how to bring its magic into your own kitchen.

## What is Congee with Century Egg?

At its heart, congee is a rice porridge, a foundational dish in many Asian cultures. It's made by simmering rice in a large amount of water or broth until the grains break down into a creamy, thick consistency. What elevates plain congee to the celebrated status of Congee with Century Egg is the addition of two key ingredients: lean pork (or often, shredded chicken) and, of course, the intriguing century egg.

The century egg, or "pidan," is a preserved duck, chicken, or quail egg that has undergone a unique curing process involving a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime, and rice hulls for several weeks or months. This process transforms the egg's appearance and flavor profile dramatically. The albumen (egg white) turns into a translucent, dark brown jelly, while the yolk takes on a creamy, dark green or gray hue with an intense, savory, and slightly ammonia-like aroma that is surprisingly appealing when balanced with other flavors. In congee, the century egg provides a rich umami punch, a slightly gelatinous texture, and a distinctive flavor that is absolutely essential to this classic dish. Paired with the tender pork and ginger, it creates a symphony of textures and tastes that is both complex and incredibly satisfying.

## Ingredients You'll Need

Creating a delicious bowl of Congee with Century Egg requires a few simple, yet specific, components. Quality ingredients will make all the difference.

*   **For the Congee Base:**
    *   1 cup medium-grain or short-grain white rice (e.g., Jasmine rice)
    *   8-10 cups cold water or chicken/pork broth (broth adds more flavor)
    *   1-inch piece of ginger, sliced thinly or smashed
    *   1/2 teaspoon salt, or to taste
    *   Optional: 1/4 teaspoon white pepper

*   **For the Century Egg & Pork:**
    *   2-3 century eggs (pidan), peeled and cut into small wedges or diced
    *   1/2 lb lean pork loin or tenderloin, thinly sliced or shredded
    *   1 tablespoon soy sauce (for marinating pork)
    *   1 teaspoon cornstarch (for marinating pork)
    *   1/2 teaspoon sesame oil (for marinating pork)

*   **For Garnish (Optional but Recommended):**
    *   2-3 green onions (scallions), thinly sliced
    *   A drizzle of sesame oil
    *   A dash of white pepper
    *   A splash of light soy sauce
    *   Chili oil, for those who like a kick

## Step-by-Step Instructions

Making Congee with Century Egg is more about patience than complex techniques. Follow these steps for a comforting bowl:

1.  **Prepare the Rice:** Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold water until the water runs clear. This removes excess starch, preventing the congee from becoming too gummy. For an even creamier texture and faster cooking time, you can soak the rice in water for 30 minutes to an hour, or even freeze it overnight (the freezing helps break down the grains).

2.  **Start the Congee:** In a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, combine the rinsed rice, 8 cups of cold water (or broth), and the ginger slices. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat, then immediately reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer gently.

3.  **Cook the Congee:** Continue to simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom of the pot. The longer it simmers, the creamier the congee will become. If the congee gets too thick, add the remaining 1-2 cups of water or broth, a little at a time, until you reach your desired consistency.

4.  **Prepare the Pork:** While the congee simmers, prepare the pork. Slice or shred the lean pork into small, bite-sized pieces. In a small bowl, marinate the pork with soy sauce, cornstarch, and sesame oil. Let it sit for at least 15 minutes.

5.  **Prepare the Century Eggs:** Carefully peel the century eggs. The easiest way is to crack them gently all around, then peel under running water. Cut them into small wedges or dice them.

6.  **Add Pork and Century Eggs:** Once the congee has reached your desired creamy consistency, increase the heat to medium-low. Add the marinated pork to the congee, stirring gently to separate the pieces. Cook for about 5-7 minutes, or until the pork is cooked through. Then, add most of the diced century eggs, reserving a few for garnish. Stir to combine.

7.  **Season and Serve:** Season the Congee with Century Egg with salt and white pepper to taste. Ladle the hot congee into individual bowls. Garnish with fresh green onions, the reserved century egg pieces, a drizzle of sesame oil, and an optional splash of soy sauce or chili oil. Serve immediately.

## Tips for Perfect Congee

*   **Rice-to-Water Ratio:** A good starting point is 1 cup of rice to 8-10 cups of liquid. Adjust based on your preferred thickness.
*   **Stirring is Key:** Stir every 15-20 minutes, especially during the latter half of cooking, to prevent sticking and encourage even creaminess.
*   **Use Broth for Flavor:** While water works, chicken or pork broth significantly enhances the depth of flavor.
*   **Don't Rush It:** True congee takes time. Low and slow simmering is essential for the rice grains to break down properly.
*   **Pre-soak or Freeze Rice:** Soaking or freezing rice can cut down on cooking time and yield a creamier texture.
*   **Adjust Consistency:** If your congee is too thick, add more hot water or broth. If it's too thin, simmer uncovered for a bit longer.

## Serving Suggestions

Congee with Century Egg is a meal in itself, but it truly shines when paired with traditional Chinese breakfast accompaniments.

*   **Youtiao (Chinese Crullers):** These crispy fried dough sticks are perfect for dipping into the warm congee.
*   **Pickled Vegetables:** A small side of pickled radish or mustard greens adds a refreshing, tangy crunch that cuts through the richness.
*   **Shredded Ginger:** Fresh matchstick ginger can be added as a garnish for an extra aromatic kick.
*   **Light Dim Sum:** Small steamed buns, dumplings, or spring rolls can complement the congee beautifully.

## Variations & Substitutions

The beauty of congee lies in its versatility. While Congee with Century Egg is a classic, don't hesitate to experiment.

*   **Meats:** Instead of pork, try shredded cooked chicken, thinly sliced fish (often added at the very end to cook quickly), or even minced beef.
*   **Vegetarian:** Omit the meat and add sliced mushrooms (shiitake or oyster), silken tofu, or finely diced carrots for a vegetarian version. You can also use vegetable broth instead of meat broth.
*   **Flavor Boosters:** Dried scallops (soaked and shredded) or dried oysters can be added to the congee base for an incredible depth of umami flavor. Add them at the beginning with the rice.
*   **Garnishes:** Beyond green onions, consider cilantro, crispy fried shallots, or a sprinkle of roasted peanuts for added texture.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does a century egg taste like?**
A century egg has a complex, savory, and slightly pungent flavor with a creamy, almost custardy yolk and a firm, gelatinous white. It doesn't taste like a "rotten" egg, but rather has a distinct umami richness that complements other ingredients beautifully.

**Is Congee with Century Egg healthy?**
Yes, it can be quite healthy! Congee is easily digestible, low in fat (especially with lean pork), and provides sustained energy. The century egg, while unique, is generally consumed in moderation. It's a nourishing and comforting meal, especially when made with a homemade broth.

**Can I make congee ahead of time?**
Absolutely! Congee can be made a day in advance and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3-4 days. When reheating, you'll likely need to add a splash of water or broth to thin it out, as it tends to thicken as it cools. Reheat gently over low heat, stirring frequently.

**What kind of rice is best for congee?**
Medium-grain or short-grain white rice, like Jasmine rice, is generally preferred for its ability to break down and create a creamy texture. Long-grain rice can also be used but might result in a slightly less creamy consistency.

**Where can I buy century eggs?**
Century eggs are readily available in most Asian grocery stores. They are usually sold in packages of 4-6 and do not require refrigeration until opened.

Congee with Century Egg is more than just a dish; it's a culinary experience that offers comfort, flavor, and a glimpse into the heart of Chinese breakfast traditions. With its velvety texture, savory pork, and the distinctive notes of century egg, it's a truly satisfying meal that promises to warm you from the inside out. Don't be intimidated by the unique ingredient; embrace the adventure and discover your new favorite Chinese breakfast recipe. Happy cooking!
